question.text: A portfolio manager at Saraswati Private Equity Fund is pitching an LP on a classic 'pure-play private equity' strategy vs a venture capital strategy. Per NISM Chapter 2.3.2, which statement BEST captures the CONVENTIONAL distinction?

answer.text: Venture capital is always illegal in India without RBI approval, while PE is SEBI-regulated.
PE invests only in listed companies, while VC invests only in unlisted companies.

Pure-play PE provides growth capital to later-stage unlisted companies with established business models and track records, while venture capital finances early-stage, unproven businesses with higher mortality risk.
PE and VC are identical in strategy; the only difference is the size of the cheque.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Series XIX-C p.36 (Ch 2.3.2), private equity is predominantly used to denote investment in companies with established business models and track records (later-stage companies), and pure-play PE provides growth capital to later-stage unlisted companies. Per p.35 (Ch 2.3.1), VC targets infant or early-stage businesses that are yet to grow or evolve, with a high mortality rate. This stage-of-investee contrast is the conventional distinction. The Trap: Option A is wrong because VC in India is SEBI-regulated as a Cat I AIF sub-category. Option B (the listed-only PE vs unlisted-only VC framing) is incorrect because both PE and VC predominantly invest in unlisted companies. Option D ignores the stage-of-investee distinction that is the entire point. Note: The conventional distinction is stage-of-investee, sourced directly from p.35-p.36.
